adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Chile - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's Chile country overview dates the national framework every regional visitor stands under: Gender Identity Law 21.120 (introduced 2013, enacted 2018, operative 2019) lets transgender people aged 14 and over change their name and sex on all official documents without requiring therapy or sex-reassignment surgery; the anti-discrimination law enacted in 2012 (Zamudio Law) protects sexual orientation and gender identity, extended to gender expression in 2018, and allows citizens to file anti-discrimination lawsuits; same-sex marriage and joint adoption by same-sex couples have been legal since 10 March 2022 (law approved 9 December 2021), following the 2015 civil union. It independently confirms the record's national-frame claims (Gender Identity Law 21.120 in force 2019, marriage since 2022, anti-discrimination law) with dates and a document-change mechanism directly relevant to a traveller whose identity papers must match their presentation.

adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Colombia - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's Colombia country overview confirms the dated national baseline a visitor to Meta stands under: consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981; the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in April 2016, making Colombia the fourth Latin American country to do so, and same-sex couples have had full adoption rights since 2015; a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation; the right to change legal gender is recognised since 1993 and without psychiatric or physical evaluations; a national LGBTI policy text addresses rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict and says national entities may not refuse to recognise them. The page carries no Meta-specific content, so it supplies only the framework against which the record's 'no Meta-specific finding' assessment and its armed-conflict displacement dynamic sit.
